evidence: Compared DRAFT with SOURCE (IC-A14, the card he approved) word by word. SOURCE: 'But before you decide where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or what it wants. It could also be your inner child, mad that you took so long to come back, or your inherited parent script, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.' DRAFT: 'Before figuring out what/where it is, make sure to ask what it is trying to stop or what it wants. It may, of course, be your inner child, mad that it’s taken you so long to come back, or it may be your inherited parent script, or something from earlier in the day, or a bit of each.' KEPT, in his order: hold off on naming it; ask what it is trying to stop and what it wants (both questions, same order); then the four possibilities (inner child mad about the long wait to come back, inherited parent script, something from earlier today, a bit of each), ending on the card's own words 'a bit of each' (not Emulate's 'a combination'), as the_change says. Two sentences, as the_change says. DIFFERENCES, all Emulate's wording, each checked for a change of claim, condition, person, number, strength or who does what: (1) 'But' dropped; the pivot is carried by 'Before ..., make sure to ask', so I count it a lost connective only. (2) 'before you decide where it’s coming from' becomes 'Before figuring out what/where it is': same step in the same place (don't name it yet); 'coming from' (origin) becomes 'what/where it is' (identity or place), but the next sentence lists exactly the candidate sources, so the reader is given the same task, not a new one. (3) 'ask it what it's trying to stop' becomes 'make sure to ask what it is trying to stop': the object 'it' is gone, so who is asked is no longer spelled out. I judged this does not change who does what: both questions are still about 'it', and the paragraph right after opens '(To the guard, in the same Nurturer voice ...', which says to speak to the thing itself; 'make sure to' is emphasis, not a new condition. Putting 'ask it' back would be cheap if the writer wants it, but I do not find it needed for the meaning. (4) 'could also be' becomes 'may, of course, be': 'also' (in addition to the guard named just above) is lost, and 'of course' adds an attitude, that the inner child is an expected possibility, which the paragraph just above sets up ('you might find yourself expecting that ... you'll find your inner child'); it is not a claim. (5) 'that you took so long' becomes 'that it’s taken you so long': same meaning; the expletive 'it' resolves at once from 'taken you so long to come back'. (6) 'or your inherited parent script' becomes 'or it may be your inherited parent script': structure only. (7) 'earlier today' becomes 'earlier in the day': same. Nothing is added that he did not say (no new claim, condition, person or number) and nothing is missing that the change says it restores. IN CONTEXT: after 'Often they are you experiencing a very charming guard. It's what protects you ...' the two sentences read in order; the possibilities list has the same 'it might just be hunger, or ..., or ...' shape as his own first paragraph of the section, so it is not foreign to the page; and the '(To the guard ...' paragraph follows. TELLS: the writer's ledger quotes only the opening of the draft in every row and its T15 line says the draft puts back his words, but only 'a bit of each' is put back, so I applied T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 myself to both sentences; none is PRESENT. Closest calls, rejected: T07 ('of course', 'make sure to' and 'what/where' sound like spoken asides, but 'of course' answers the expectation his paragraph just above sets up, so it comes from a thought-turn, not a staged filler); T15 (same skeleton and order as the card, but the swaps go to plainer spoken forms, not rarer words, and no other tell rides through); T22 (it instructs, but it holds a stance, ask before deciding, and 'mad that it’s taken you so long' is a human detail, not reassurance); T02 (the paragraph is a run of short verdict, instruction and distinction sentences, but its first four are his own and the draft swaps two sentences for two without adding a compressed command); T12 and T21 (the possibilities are an open enumeration of sources, the approved card's own, not a tidy taxonomy or several argumentative jobs); T20 and T29 ('or a bit of each' is a casual catch-all and a new consideration, the card's, not a clever closer or a moral); C02 (the reaction 'it' and the expletive 'it’s taken' do not collide in reading). LINTER: 'B4/E15 list or packed sentence' accepted: the long sentence is the approved card's own list of possible sources, each a separate claim of his, and the draft gives the items different shapes (the child with why it is mad, 'it may be' for the script, a bare noun phrase, then the catch-all). 'D9 follows the source order' accepted: it rewrites the two sentences it replaces, so it follows their order by design; I checked T13 and T09 as the finding asks, and 'mad that it’s taken you so long to come back' is where something is noticed. 'E125 list of three' accepted: the meaning needs every item (dropping one would drop a possibility he approved), the items have different shapes, and the list ends on his catch-all 'a bit of each'.
